title: Hidden Lake Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Hidden Lake wells have a 245 ft median depth, with finished-well costs estimated at $21,900-$36,500.
h1: What Hidden Lake Wells Cost, Produce, and Require
intro_html:
Buying land near Hidden Lake means understanding fractured mountain bedrock, not just looking at a nearby well location. Records within 5 miles show a median well depth of 245 feet, but the middle half runs from 110 to 400 feet. Reported yields are generally usable, although drilling results can vary sharply from one lot to the next.

This page uses Colorado DWR permit records for Boulder County, including Bark Ranch, Ward, Gold Hill, Jamestown, Sunshine, and Crisman. It also covers the practical questions that matter before closing or starting construction: depth, flow, water levels, drilling cost, septic planning, and environmental due diligence.

sections.heading: Hidden Lake well depths reflect fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
The 700 wells with reported total depth have a median of 245 feet. The middle half is 110 to 400 feet, which gives a driller a reasonable local range but not a guaranteed target. About 21% are under 100 feet, 34% are 100 to 300 feet, 35% are 300 to 600 feet, and 10% exceed 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,428 feet.

That spread is typical of a mountain bedrock setting. Most permits name an unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer, with smaller numbers identifying fractured crystalline or fractured granite zones. A bid based only on the median can miss a difficult hole, so ask how the contractor handles extra footage, casing, grouting, and an unsuccessful water-bearing zone.

sections.heading: Most Hidden Lake wells report useful household flow
sections.html:
Only 351 wells report a pump yield, so the yield data is not a complete measure of every permitted well. Among those records, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 5.0 to 7.0 gallons per minute. The distribution is 3% under 1 gallon per minute, 21% from 1 to 5, 68% from 5 to 15, and 7% above 15.

For a typical household, that pattern is encouraging, but flow rate is not the same as storage or dependable daily supply. A low-yield well may still work with a storage tank and careful demand management. Confirm the well permit's allowed use, test the actual well, and have the pump and pressure system sized for the lot and proposed home.

sections.heading: Water levels are deeper in the newer Hidden Lake records
sections.html:
Only 39 wells report a static water level, so treat the water-level sample as limited. The median depth to water is 55 feet, with the middle half from 25 to 100 feet below the surface. Measurements from the 2010s show a median of 32 feet, while measurements from the 2020s show 100 feet.

That decade comparison suggests deeper measured water levels in the newer records, but it does not by itself prove a basin-wide declining water table. Different locations, seasons, well depths, and measurement methods can affect the result. Before buying, request the neighboring well records and ask for a current static-level measurement and a production test on the property well.

sections.heading: Permit history shows long use and active local drillers
sections.html:
The records include 1,111 permitted wells, with 732 marked as constructed and 700 reporting total depth. Permits were issued across the decades, including 197 in the 1970s, 154 in the 1980s, 220 in the 1990s, 136 in the 2000s, 90 in the 2010s, and 48 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

Most permits are for domestic or household use, at 89%; stock use is 2%, irrigation is 1%, and monitoring is 4%. The most active drillers in these records are Ground Water Systems Inc. (Wilson, Richard R.), Ingram Drilling Inc. (Ingram, Stephen E.), and Norris & Sons (Norris, T A). Confirm current licensing, availability, and references rather than assuming historical activity means a current recommendation.

sections.heading: A median-depth Hidden Lake well can cost $21,900-$36,500
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss, at $65 to $100 per foot. At the 245-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $15,900 to $24,500. A finished well, including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical, is estimated at $21,900 to $36,500.

Those figures are planning numbers, not a fixed proposal. A well reaching 600 feet or more can move well beyond the median budget, and difficult access can add work that is not captured by footage alone. Get the drilling rate, casing and grout assumptions, mobilization, water testing, pump installation, trenching, electrical scope, and dry-hole terms in writing before you compare bids.

sections.heading: Check contamination, dry-hole risk, and septic layout before closing
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 717 historic mine features, and 58 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped features do not establish contamination at a particular parcel, but they are a reason to review site history, mine maps, groundwater direction, and available testing before relying on a well.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible in fractured granite or gneiss, even where nearby wells produce well. A septic system also needs suitable soil, reserve area, driveway access, and separation from the well. Have the well location, septic field, building envelope, access drive, and utility trench reviewed together. Check the DWR permit and any augmentation or use restrictions before construction, especially if the planned use is more than ordinary household use.

sections.heading: Use nearby well records before buying a Hidden Lake lot
sections.html:
Start with the property well permit, construction report, pump information, water-quality results, and recent production history. Then compare nearby records in Bark Ranch, Ward, Gold Hill, Jamestown, Sunshine, and Crisman. The local depth and yield ranges are useful for a first budget, but they cannot replace a site-specific test because fractured bedrock conditions can change over short distances.

For a vacant lot, make the contract contingent on confirming a legal water supply, a workable well location, and an approved septic concept. For an existing home, inspect the pressure tank, pump controls, storage, electrical service, and wellhead. If the proposed use changes, ask Colorado DWR whether the permit allows it; an exempt household-use well is not automatically a source for every future use.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Hidden Lake, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Hidden Lake is 245 feet. The middle half runs from 110 to 400 feet, while 10% of reported wells are deeper than 600 feet. The deepest record is 1,428 feet. Because the area is fractured mountain bedrock, a neighboring well gives useful context but cannot guarantee the depth on your parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Hidden Lake?
faq.a: The local model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured granite or gneiss. At the 245-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $15,900 to $24,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $21,900 to $36,500. Greater depth, difficult access, or extra construction can increase the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Hidden Lake wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 351 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 5.0 to 7.0. About 3% report under 1 gallon per minute, while 68% report 5 to 15. These figures describe reported wells, not a guarantee. Test the property well and review storage and pump capacity before buying.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Hidden Lake?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from a permit or a neighboring well. Within about 10 miles, records show 6 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 717 historic mine features, and 58 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove a problem at your parcel. Test the well for relevant contaminants, review site history, and retest if conditions or ownership change.

faq.q: Are Hidden Lake water levels getting lower?
faq.a: The limited static-level records show a median depth to water of 55 feet, with a middle half of 25 to 100 feet. By measurement decade, the median was 32 feet below surface in the 2010s and 100 feet in the 2020s. That suggests deeper recent measurements, but the sample is only 39 wells and does not prove a regional decline.
